doc.title: Ruth Brisbane interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 2, 2013

title: Anatomy of a club show and exotic dancers
summary: The running order of emcee, dancer and singer, her sister-in-law's act, and the hours worked.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: And what would define an exotic dancer? What made them exotic?

Their costumes. It was in quote stripping. But they had an act. It was really hilarious and I’d love to see on Sanford & Son, his cousin or, she used to be an exotic dancer. She was very funny, the woman. I can’t think of her name. And I heard that she used a snake. Yes. She was a snake charmer. That was her hook. My sister-in-law stripped from a costume that was — and music too — “The Last Time I Saw Paris.” And she came out in a couture suit and from there she stripped, which she was a gorgeous woman, beautiful. And very classy. She had a very classy act.
Did you get to sing before or after the stripper?
The stripper was usually on in the middle, yes. And the emcee and comedian would come out and tell the jokes at the beginning and then more, and I think the singer usually was last.
And how many shows did you do a night?
Oh at least three or four.
So the hours typically would have been —
From about ten to four in the morning. From ten P.M. to four in the morning. And in New York they closed at three so it would be from ten to three. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
